Lesson 65 assumed forty trades a month and said the forty was not derived. Measured on the grid this course has been running, 80.63 per cent of rules fire twice or less, and the book asks for nothing on fifteen days in twenty-eight.

Lesson 65 turned a trade count into a wait by assuming forty trades a month, and said in the same breath that the forty was stated rather than derived. Measure it instead, on the 253-cell grid every lesson since 63 has been running. Over the stretch each rule is defined on, 138 of the 253 produce exactly one entry, 80.63 per cent produce two or fewer, and the busiest cell in the whole grid works out at seventy-five entries a year. Lesson 67 needed 589 trades to settle whether a tenth of an R was real. At the busiest rule’s pace that is just under eight years, and at the median rule’s it is longer than a working life. The day is not short of hours. It is short of decisions: over the twenty-eight moves where lesson 71’s four rules are all defined, the book asks for an order on thirteen days and for nothing on fifteen, and never for two rules on the same day.

Read the first column down. Thirteen orders in twenty-eight days, and nine of the thirteen come from one rule. The 2-and-5 crossing generates 69.23 per cent of the book’s workload, and lesson 73 gave that same rule the largest weight it could hold, 0.630. Those two facts are the same fact. Look at the third column of lesson 73’s inputs: 2-and-5 had the lowest standard deviation of the four, 0.6375 against 0.7218, 0.7265 and 0.7032, and it had it because it holds a position on nineteen days of the twenty-eight while the others hold on twenty-one to twenty-five. Being out of the market more often is what made it quiet, being quiet is what won it the weight, and being out of the market more often is also what makes it flip. The rule with most of your money in it is the rule with most of your day in it, by construction rather than by luck.

Read the third column and the fourth together, and mistrust the fourth. Turning one entry in twenty-eight moves into nine entries a year is arithmetic performed on a single event, and no single row of that column should be quoted. The aggregate is what carries weight: across all 253 cells, on the stretch each is defined on, 138 of them fired once, eighty-three fired twice or three times, and thirty-two fired more than three, the busiest reaching sixteen. The distribution, not any row of it, is what says the pace is nearer half a dozen entries a year than forty a month.

Now the same grid on the shared window, which is where the day comes from. The 253 rules produce 437 orders over the twenty-eight days, an average of 1.73 each, and 80.63 per cent of them ask for at most one order in the whole stretch. And here is the number that stops this from being an argument for idleness: run all 253 and only one of the twenty-eight days is quiet. A full day’s work is available. It costs exactly what lesson 75 priced it at, which is a quartering of the size per trade for a day 2.86 per cent smaller.

The first four rows are twelve operations for a four-rule book: two averages and one comparison per rule, plus a division and a count on the days an order exists. On fifteen of the twenty-eight days all twelve return yesterday’s answer. Lesson 69 measured the delay a person inserts between the signal and the order; this table is what that delay is being inserted into, and it is twelve operations that a spreadsheet finishes before you have found the chart.

The last two rows are the ones that feel like the day’s real work and are not daily at all. Lesson 67’s 589 trades arrive at the pace measured above, which on the busiest rule in the grid is just under eight years. A daily review cannot decide whether a rule still works, because the evidence needed for that decision does not arrive daily. What it can decide is whether the twelve operations ran, whether the order that should have gone out went out, and whether the count in lesson 75’s fourth column is still what you think it is.

Module 10 keeps a running list of what the day contains that is not the decision, and this page opens it with one item: the twelve operations, and the fifteen days in twenty-eight on which they change nothing.

The thirteen order days do not arrive evenly. They fall on moves 36, 39, 40, 42, 44, 45, then a gap, then 52 to 56 consecutively, then 58 and 59. So the window contains a six-day stretch with no order in it and, immediately after, five consecutive days each of which needs one. Take those two stretches against each other, on the 2-and-5 rule, which produced all five of the busy days.

Moves 46 to 51, six days: the position never changes, no order is sent, and the rule earns 0.30 in the instrument’s units. A typical daily move here is the average absolute move over the same twenty-eight, which is 0.7286, so 0.30 is 0.41 of one.
Moves 52 to 56, five days: exit, entry, exit, entry, exit. Five orders in five sessions, and the rule earns 1.00, which is 1.37 typical daily moves.

The busy week made more than three times what the quiet one made, and it made it by holding nothing on the two days the instrument fell and holding on the day it rose 1.30. The instrument itself rose 0.90 across those five days, so the rule beat holding it. Every crossing is real and every order is correct under the rule, and none of that decides whether the week was worth having, because that is decided in the bill.

Now price the five orders, which is two and a half round trips, using lesson 12’s two ends. On lesson 12’s index ETF, where a round trip costs a fifth of one per cent of a typical day’s movement, the five orders cost 0.0036 against a gain of 1.00, so the week keeps 99.6 per cent of what it made. On lesson 12’s micro cap, where a round trip costs 52 per cent of a day’s movement, the same five orders cost 0.95 and the week keeps 0.05, a twentieth of the gain and seven hundredths of one typical day’s movement. Identical rule, identical week, identical orders, and the only thing that changed is the instrument lesson 12 told you to choose first.

Read the two stretches against the feeling each produces. The six quiet days feel like a system that has stopped working and are worth four tenths of one day’s movement, which is about what they look like. The five busy days feel like a working week, and on the index ETF they are one. On the micro cap they are the same five correct orders keeping a twentieth of the same gain. The feeling is identical in both cases and it is not tracking anything.

That one entry in twenty-eight moves is a pace. It is one event on one stretch of one instrument, and the sixty closes this course carries are far too few to estimate any single rule’s frequency. What survives that objection is the aggregate and its order of magnitude: 138 of 253 cells fired once and 80.63 per cent fired twice or less, on windows of twenty-eight to fifty-five moves. That is not consistent with forty trades a month by any reading, and the gap is a factor of tens rather than a rounding.

That the annual column should be quoted. It should not. Every row of it multiplies a count of one or seven by a constant, and a count of one has a standard error about the size of itself. The column exists so that 480 entries a year, which is what lesson 65’s forty trades a month comes to, can be set beside 33.3 and 6.6 without arithmetic in the reader’s head. Use the distribution instead, and treat every yearly figure on this page as arithmetic rather than as measurement.

That doing nothing and knowing nothing are the same. On the fifteen quiet days the twelve operations still have to run and the answer still has to be looked at, because the difference between a day with no order and a day where the order was missed is invisible from the outside and is exactly the difference this page cannot see in your record either. An idle day is monitored. An unmonitored day only looks idle.
